items.readable_text:
Content:
The side-angle-side (SAS) similarity criterion can be used as a shortcut to prove that two triangles are similar. It states the following:

Content:
> Two triangles are similar if the ratio of the lengths of two pairs of corresponding sides is the same, and the angles included by these sides are congruent.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the two triangles shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/423d4d678d4595432188ec0e8eb6ff91]

Content:
We see that we have a pair of congruent angles,
[MATH: \angle{B}\cong \angle{F}.]

Content:
Also, the ratios of the side lengths that include these congruent angles are equal.

Content:
[MATH: (AB)/(EF)|= (4)/(8) = (1)/(2); (BC)/(FG)|= (5)/(10) = (1)/(2)]

Content:
Therefore, the SAS criterion guarantees that the two triangles are similar, and we can write

Content:
[MATH: \triangle ABC \sim \triangle EFG .]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The SAS (side-angle-side) similarity criterion states the following:

Two triangles are similar if the ratio of the lengths of two pairs of corresponding sides is the same, and the angles included by these sides are congruent.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given triangles.

  • [MATH: \mathcal{P}] is similar to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SAS since the ratios of the lengths of the sides corresponding to the congruent angles are equal: [MATH: \dfrac{6}{4}=\dfrac{3}{2}]

  • [MATH: \mathcal{Q}] is similar to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SAS since the ratios of the lengths of the sides corresponding to the congruent angles are equal: [MATH: \dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{12}{8}]

  • [MATH: \mathcal{R}] is not similar to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SAS since the ratios of the lengths of the sides corresponding to the congruent angles are not equal: [MATH: \dfrac{6}{3}\neq\dfrac{8}{8}]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \mathcal{P}] and [MATH: \mathcal{Q}] only."

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: \overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD},] we have that [MATH: \angle ACD \cong \angle CAB]

since they are alternate interior angles.

Moreover, the lengths of the sides enclosing the congruent angles are in proportion:

[MATH: (AB)/(AC)|= (8)/(6) = (4)/(3); (AC)/(CD)|= (6)/(4.5) = (4)/(3)]

So, by the SAS similarity criterion, we have that [MATH: \triangle BAC\sim \triangle ACD.] As a result, the ratios of all the corresponding sides must be the same. Therefore,

[MATH: (BC)/(DA)|= (4)/(3); (x)/(3)|= (4)/(3); x|= (4)/(3) ⋅ 3; = 4.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The side-angle-side (SAS) similarity criterion can be used as a shortcut to prove that two triangles are similar. It states the following:

Content:
> Two triangles are similar if the ratio of the lengths of two pairs of corresponding sides is the same, and the angles included by these sides are congruent.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the two triangles shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/423d4d678d4595432188ec0e8eb6ff91]

Content:
We see that we have a pair of congruent angles,
[MATH: \angle{B}\cong \angle{F}.]

Content:
Also, the ratios of the side lengths that include these congruent angles are equal.

Content:
[MATH: (AB)/(EF)|= (4)/(8) = (1)/(2); (BC)/(FG)|= (5)/(10) = (1)/(2)]

Content:
Therefore, the SAS criterion guarantees that the two triangles are similar, and we can write

Content:
[MATH: \triangle ABC \sim \triangle EFG .]

---

> Two triangles are similar if the ratio of the lengths of two pairs of corresponding sides is the same, and the angles included by these sides are congruent.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the given triangles.

- [MATH: \mathcal{P}] is similar to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SAS since the ratios of the lengths of the sides corresponding to the congruent angles are equal: [MATH: \dfrac{6}{4}=\dfrac{3}{2}]
- [MATH: \mathcal{Q}] is similar to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SAS since the ratios of the lengths of the sides corresponding to the congruent angles are equal: [MATH: \dfrac{9}{6} = \dfrac{12}{8}]
- [MATH: \mathcal{R}] is not similar to [MATH: \mathcal{T}] by SAS since the ratios of the lengths of the sides corresponding to the congruent angles are not equal: [MATH: \dfrac{6}{3}\neq\dfrac{8}{8}]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \mathcal{P}] and [MATH: \mathcal{Q}] only."
